title: Research Bite #53: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #53 covers Ewan Murray, Aidan J. Horner, and Silke M. Göbel's 'A Meta-analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning,' published in Educational Psychology Review (2025, Vol. 37, Article 75). The team synthesized the mathematics-specific evidence for two of the best-known learning strategies -- spacing (distributing practice across sessions rather than massing it) and retrieval practice (actively recalling rather than re-studying) -- pooling 27 studies and 53 effect sizes for the spacing comparison. They found a robust small-to-medium benefit for spaced over massed practice overall (g = 0.28), and the effect was stronger for isolated skills (g = 0.38) than for material embedded within an ongoing course sequence (g = 0.24). The evidence for retrieval practice specifically in mathematics, by contrast, was inconclusive -- not because it doesn't work, but because too few dedicated studies exist to draw a confident conclusion, unlike the well-established literature on retrieval practice in verbal/factual domains. Barton's takeaway is that spacing is safe to bank on for maths instruction now, while retrieval practice in maths remains promising but not yet proven at the same evidentiary standard.
points: The effect-size gap between isolated material (g = 0.38) and course-embedded material (g = 0.24) suggests spacing pays off most when a skill is practiced as a standalone unit rather than folded continuously into new content -- a scheduling detail, not just a philosophy.

The meta-analysis's honest null-to-inconclusive verdict on retrieval practice in mathematics is itself a high-impact finding: it cautions against assuming results from verbal-memory retrieval-practice research transfer automatically to maths.

With only 27 studies and 53 effect sizes underpinning the spacing conclusion, this is a real but still modest evidence base compared to more heavily studied domains -- confident application should stay proportionate to that base.

For maths departments building a spiral/interleaved curriculum, the finding functions as an evidentiary endorsement of spacing recently taught topics into later units, not just isolated revision sessions.

The distinction Barton draws out -- massed practice as the common default in maths homework/revision, spaced practice as the evidence-backed alternative -- gives teachers a concrete, low-cost redesign target.
quotes: This meta-analysis synthesizes existing research to examine the effectiveness of spacing and retrieval practice in mathematics education. The authors investigate whether spreading out study sessions (spacing) or actively recalling information (retrieval practice) improves mathematics learning compared to massed practice or restudying.
Their findings suggest that spaced practice generally enhances mathematics retention, with a more pronounced effect for isolated concepts versus material embedded in a course.
However, the evidence for the robust impact of retrieval practice alone in mathematics is inconclusive, potentially due to a limited number of dedicated studies.

Teachers should remember that spacing out mathematics practice over multiple sessions robustly improves learning and retention, for both isolated material and within a course. While retrieval practice shows promise, its effect in mathematics learning is not yet conclusively robust.

Interleaving: The practice of mixing different topics and skills during practice sessions. Spacing Effect (Distributed Practice): Spreading out practice over multiple sessions, which leads to better retention compared to massed practice.
